the accelerated progression of atherosclerotic lesions in this case seems linked principally to a chronic state of immune activation, which is not directly related to classical risk factors.

the presence of atherosclerotic plaques in HIV-infected patients is not a simple consequence of the presence of traditional risk factors, but is also due to a complex interplay between HIV, its viral and cellular products, and the immune response to the virus.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the rapid progression of atherosclerotic disease in HIV patients is associated with the presence of chronic immune activation and chronic inflammation, and the presence of other factors, such as chronic C hepatitis, iritable bowel syndrome, and PCI execution, may be able to contribute to the development of atherosclerosic disease.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the presence of HIV infection and HCV coinfection should be taken into account when considering a patient for PCI, because the risk for accelerated progression of coronary disease may be greater in these subjects.
